doc.title: Bill Crow interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Army friends introduce traditional jazz and bebop
summary: In the Army in Baltimore a moldy fig teaches him Armstrong repertoire, and a Massillon bebopper brings him to Dave Garroway's radio show and bebop.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: So when I got into the Army, first I came under the influence of this moldy fig who taught me that whole repertoire which has stood me in great good stead as a professional musician, because I know all of the Armstrong stuff, the traditional Chicago jazz tunes. And then another guy came in from Massillon, Ohio, who was a Bebopper. And we said, “What’s Bebop, we don’t know—” And he said, “Well there’s a station out of Chicago late at night we can probably get.” We were stationed in Baltimore at that time. So we would stay up at night and get the Dave Garroway show. And Dave was the disc jockey at that time in Chicago who liked Sarah Vaughan and George Treadwell’s arrangements, and Charlie Parker, and the more melodic stuff. He didn’t really go into the outside music. But that was my first taste. And it sounded wonderful to me. I’d been listening to

classical composers that used that kind of harmony anyway, Ravel and Debussy and Mahler. So it just seemed like a natural addition to what I was already listening to but my moldy fig friend was outraged. He said, “You can’t like that music!” I said, “How do I stop myself?” So I didn’t see why I couldn’t play both kinds, and I have to this day.
